annotations.target_phrase: sad and weary I go back to you, my cold father
annotations.annotation_text: Anna Livia Plurabelle (ALP) speaking in her dying monologue as she flows out into the cold, bitter Irish Sea / Atlantic Ocean, addressing her father the Ocean.
sources: Bishop, John. Joyce's Book of the Dark. https://archive.org/details/joycesbookofdark0000bish
Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp

annotations.target_phrase: moyles and moyles of it, moananoaning, makes me seasilt saltsick
annotations.annotation_text: Miles and miles + the Sea of Moyle (where the Children of Lir were transformed into swans for 300 years in Irish legend). The brackish mix of fresh river water with ocean brine.
sources: Joyce, P.W. Old Celtic Romances (The Fate of the Children of Lir). https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/34190

annotations.target_phrase: Avelaval. My leaves have drifted from me
annotations.annotation_text: Blends "Ave" (Hail / farewell in Latin), "vale" (goodbye), and "laval" (washing, French laver). ALP's autumnal leaves shedding into the river stream as life ebbs away.
sources: Virgil. Aeneid (Book VI: The Falling Leaves). https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/vergil/aen6.shtml

annotations.target_phrase: Carry me along, taddy, like you done through the toy fair!
annotations.annotation_text: Childhood memory of her father carrying her through the Dublin Donnybrook / Peter's toy fair, evoking the filial intimacy between the dying soul and the paternal source.
sources: O'Donovan, John. The Annals of the Four Masters. https://celt.ucc.ie/published/T100005A/

annotations.target_phrase: under whitespread wings like he'd come from Arkangels
annotations.annotation_text: Sea gull wings and the Archangel Michael coming to receive the departing spirit at death.
sources: Dante Alighieri. Purgatorio (Canto II: The Angelic Boatman). https://dante.mcl.ac.uk/

annotations.target_phrase: Whish! A gull. Gulls. Far calls. Coming, far!
annotations.annotation_text: Auditory manifestation of the gulls screaming over Dublin Bay, calling the river out to the open sea. Echoes the Four Master Annalists (Mamalujo) as four gulls.

annotations.target_phrase: Finn, again! Take. Bussoftlhee, mememormee! Till thousendsthee
annotations.annotation_text: Invocation of Finn MacCool rising again; German "Buss' oft" (kiss often) and English "be soft of thee"; "remember me" (Dido's lament in Purcell's Dido and Aeneas); thousand years cycle.
sources: Purcell, Henry. Dido and Aeneas (When I am laid in earth). https://imslp.org/wiki/Dido_and_Aeneas,_Z.626_(Purcell,_Henry)
MacKillop, James. Dictionary of Celtic Mythology: Fionn mac Cumhaill. https://www.oxfordreference.com

annotations.target_phrase: The keys to. Given! A way a lone a last a loved a long the
annotations.annotation_text: The climactic broken sentence of the novel ending on the definite article "the", which loops directly into the opening word on page 3: "riverrun, past Eve and Adam's...". Perfect circularity of Vico's ricorso and ALP's eternal return.
sources: Hart, Clive. Structure and Motif in Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/structuremotifin0000hart

annotations.annotation_text: Joyce's authorial dateline recording the seventeen years of composition from the year Ulysses was published (1922) to the completion and publication of Finnegans Wake (1939) in Paris.
sources: National Library of Ireland: James Joyce Collection. https://www.nli.ie
